findings.issue_text: Worker exceptions are logged but the offset is still marked complete in `finally`, committing failed result processing and permanently losing it.

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` flags workers to stop before queues are drained, so workers exit after their current item and leave queued work unprocessed; the commit loop is also stopped before that work can be committed.
The code uses Python 3.13-only `queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown()` despite supporting Python 3.11+, causing `AttributeError` and potentially leaving workers blocked in `get()`.
Worker queues are unbounded, so there is no natural backpressure and sustained load with slow workers can cause unbounded memory growth.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Worker exceptions are logged but the offset is still marked complete in `finally`, committing failed result processing and permanently losing it.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the OrderedQueueWorker.run() method in queue_consumer.py, the code catches exceptions in the try block but the finally block always calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)`. This means even when processing fails with an exception (logged at line 139-141), the offset is still marked as complete. This allows the offset to be committed, effectively losing the failed message permanently since it won't be reprocessed. The test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` even demonstrates this behavior - it expects that after an exception, offsets should NOT be committed, but the current implementation will mark them complete anyway.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` flags workers to stop before queues are drained, so workers exit after their current item and leave queued work unprocessed; the commit loop is also stopped before that work can be committed.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the shutdown() method in FixedQueuePool (lines 224-236), it first sets worker.shutdown = True for all workers, then calls q.shutdown(immediate=False) on queues, then joins workers. In OrderedQueueWorker.run() (lines 117-145), the worker checks self.shutdown in the while loop condition. When shutdown=True is set, after the current work_item completes, the loop exits before processing remaining queued items. The queue.shutdown(immediate=False) is called after workers are flagged to stop, so workers may exit their loop before the queue shutdown takes effect. Additionally, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins commit_thread before calling queue_pool.shutdown(), meaning the commit loop stops before remaining work is processed and committed. This could result in data loss where queued work items are never processed or committed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The code uses Python 3.13-only `queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown()` despite supporting Python 3.11+, causing `AttributeError` and potentially leaving workers blocked in `get()`.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows in queue_consumer.py lines 127-128 and 223-224 the use of `queue.ShutDown` exception and `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` method. These are Python 3.13+ features (PEP 661). The code catches `queue.ShutDown` in the worker's run() method and calls `q.shutdown()` in the FixedQueuePool.shutdown() method. If this code runs on Python 3.11 or 3.12, it will raise AttributeError since Queue.shutdown() doesn't exist and queue.ShutDown exception class doesn't exist. This is a real compatibility bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Worker queues are unbounded, so there is no natural backpressure and sustained load with slow workers can cause unbounded memory growth.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, the FixedQueuePool creates queues with `queue.Queue[WorkItem[T]] = queue.Queue()` (line ~170 in queue_consumer.py) which creates unbounded queues with no maxsize parameter. The docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' but this is incorrect since unbounded queues never fill up. While this isn't a bug per se (the code functions correctly), it's a legitimate architectural concern - under sustained load with slow workers, memory could grow unboundedly. This is a real, specific issue grounded in the diff code.
